meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Hale. Was Owen heard before you entered that zero?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
"Pretty conclusive." The company's own guide says its indicator "should not be used as the sole basis for adverse actions against a student." You didn't answer me: was Owen heard first?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. What do you have that isn't a machine's opinion?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. Owen told me he wrote it over the weekend, and a paste shows where words landed, not who wrote them. Who else has seen that screen?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
It's not on that page. A seventeen-year-old getting a quotation wrong is a citation error, Hale, not grounds for a zero. And you haven't told me who else has seen any of this.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
He changed his argument between an outline and an essay. That's called thinking. You keep adding paper and answering nothing, so yes or no: is anything on his record right now?

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

So you did speak to him first. Five minutes after class is an ambush, not a hearing, and "like, being stuck" is what it means. I want copies of those notes and the September writing, and you still owe me an answer on his record.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4. Owen will do the rewrite to put this behind him, not because he did anything, and tonight's writing says nothing is on his record now or ever. The copies I asked for will be in my email to you.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school. Who supervises, and who else is in the room?
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, on what you said, in writing tonight. Ten minutes. Now answer me: who is in that room on Thursday?
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

To: Hale
Cc: Principal, Elbow Crossing High School

Hale,

You agreed today to a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4, not in front of Owen's class, on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero, nothing placed on his record, and the mark entered well before December 1. I still require copies of your November 2 notes and his September 24 in-class writing, a plain answer on whether anything is on his record now, and the names of whoever will supervise and whoever else will be in the room. I expect your written confirmation tonight, as you said.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: Last position. She agreed to the private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, confirmed in writing tonight. She still wants copies of your notes and the September writing, a straight answer on whether anything is on his record now, and to know who will be in the room. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and you reached it before her time ran out.

What moved her: You put procedure 4.4 on the table in full, with the rewrite private, the mark replacing the zero, nothing on his record, and all of it in writing tonight. That met the one thing she never trades, after you had already shown her dated documents she could check.

What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it pretty conclusive. To her that is a machine's opinion she came prepared to knock down, and it let her skip past your greeting and go straight on the attack.

What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop. Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history came very close to that night, because it put the essay's creation at 11:31 PM on Wednesday, October 28, with the text arriving in two large edits before midnight. That proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.

Try next time: When she asked, yes or no, whether anything is on his record right now, answer it before you show the next document, because it is her biggest fear and she had to ask twice.
